title: The AI Financial Trust Spectrum: How People Are Rethinking Money Decisions in 2026
summary: AI crunches data in seconds, but can it replace humans for financial decision-making? Intuit explores where people fall on the AI financial trust spectrum.

- The AI Financial Trust Spectrum: How People Are Rethinking Money Decisions in 2026


Financial advice has traditionally come from human professionals, namely advisors and planners trained to understand nuance and guide complex decisions.[AI in finance](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/tech-innovation/artificial-intelligence-in-finance/) now offers something different: instant, on-demand guidance powered by vast datasets and advanced algorithms.


So, what does that mean for how Americans approach money decisions?


To find out, Intuit surveyed 1,000 US adults on how they’re using AI in their financial decision-making¹. Read on to learn what the data reveals about the future of financial guidance in the AI era.


**The short answer:** In 2026, 54% of respondents still prefer human financial advisors, 33% use a hybrid AI-and-human approach, and 14% prefer AI alone, according to Intuit’s survey of 1,000 US adults. Those who prefer AI report the highest financial confidence (76.4 out of 100) but are also the least likely to verify advice before acting on it (71% follow AI guidance without verification).


## **Key Findings at a Glance**


- Many respondents still prefer financial advice from human professionals (54%), but about one-third prefer a combination of human intelligence (HI) and AI advice.
- Individuals who prefer financial advice from AI had the highest average Financial Confidence Score (76.4), while those who prefer human advice had the lowest score (70.3).
- Higher confidence may come with higher risk. The study found that 71% of the individuals who prefer AI advice follow it without verification. That’s more than double the AI verification rate (33%) of those who prefer human advice.
- Among AI users, weekly use is most common (45%), but daily use is also significant (21%).
- As the stakes of financial situations increase, individuals tend to rely more heavily on guidance from human professionals.
- Respondents say proven accuracy, access to a human expert, and strong data privacy protections would increase their trust in AI financial tools.
- Consumers expect AI to supplement, not replace, human financial guidance in the years to come.


## **How Was the Financial Trust Spectrum Measured?**


The goal of this study was to determine 2 measures: the **Financial Trust Spectrum** and the **Financial Confidence Score** .


**The Financial Trust Spectrum (FTS)** is a three-tier classification that segments US adults into 3 categories based on observed financial decision-making behavior across multiple scenarios:


- Prefer a real human
- Hybrid
- Prefer AI


The segmentation reflects observed responses, not what people said they preferred in the abstract.


**The Financial Confidence Score (FCS)** is a composite index that measures how confident an individual feels about their financial decision-making across six dimensions: decision confidence, ability to evaluate advice, sense of control, preparedness, satisfaction with past decisions, and levels of worry or regret.


Scores are standardized so the 3 trust segments can be compared on equal footing. A fuller methodology breakdown appears at the end of the piece.


## **What Are the 3 Financial Decision-Making Mindsets?**


Our survey split respondents into 3 key mindsets based on the financial decision-making behaviors they reported: those who prefer to use AI for financial decisions, those who prefer to talk with a human advisor, and those who prefer a mix of the two.


**Mindset** **% of respondents** **Avg. Financial Confidence Score** **Verifies AI Advice** **Key Trait**


Prefer Human 54% 70.3 67% verify Turns to advisors for high-stakes decisions


Hybrid 33% 71.9 56% verify Cross-references AI and human advice


Prefer AI 14% 76.4 29% verify Self-directed, tech-forward, least cautious


Here’s a closer look at each.


### **Those Who Prefer a Real Human (54%): Traditional and Expertise-Focused**


Many respondents (54%) still prefer advice from a traditional financial professional, such as an advisor, accountant, or planner.


Respondents in this group said they would turn to a financial professional over an AI-powered tool in certain high-stakes situations, including unexpectedly receiving $250,000 and experiencing a 20% drop in their retirement account.


This group tends to have less financial confidence than those who prefer AI advice, a pattern that aligns with their preference for[human intelligence (HI) versus AI](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/ai-vs-human-intelligence/) in moments that feel consequential.


### **Hybrid (33%): Balanced and Validation-Oriented**


Roughly a third of respondents (33%) take a hybrid approach. This group turns to both AI and human financial professionals, often equally, when facing an important financial decision or crisis.


Unsurprisingly, they’re more likely to validate information across multiple sources. And their average confidence score falls between the scores of those who prefer AI and those who prefer human advice.


### **Those Who Prefer AI (14%): Confident and Tech-Driven**


The smallest of the 3 segments, representing 14% of respondents, leans toward AI tools over human financial professionals.


This tech-forward group is self-directed, relies on AI tools, and reports the highest levels of financial confidence. However, they’re also the least likely to verify AI advice before following it.


Nearly all with this mindset have used AI for financial questions, and they’re more likely to follow AI recommendations, even if those recommendations conflict with human advice.


## **Is AI Replacing Human Financial Advisors?**


Many respondents still prefer to receive financial advice from a human advisor, but roughly 45% of respondents expect the hybrid approach of AI and HI to prevail in the future.


### **This Shift Isn’t About Replacing Humans**


The findings push back on the idea that AI is poised to replace human financial advisors. In practice, though, respondents treat AI more as a supplemental resource than a substitute.


For example, when asked how they’d respond if an AI financial tool suggested a tax strategy that their financial advisor didn’t, 60% of respondents said they’d research both options before making a final call.


The split makes sense given the strengths of each. AI offers advantages like rapid data processing and 24/7 availability, and human advisors bring context and judgment in complex situations that data alone can’t provide.


Combining AI and human analysis in financial advisory gives Americans access to what each does well.


## **Do People Who Use AI Feel More Financially Confident?**


Along with reshaping how Americans seek financial guidance, AI is influencing how confident they feel about their financial lives.


Intuit’s Financial Confidence Score is structured to measure this impact. The FCS is based on how a person responds to questions about their confidence in financial decisions, sense of financial control over the future, satisfaction with past financial decisions, and levels of financial stress and regret.


### **Confidence Scores by Group**


The average FCS across the different groups fell within about 6 points of each other. However, there was a clear trend: A higher preference for AI guidance correlated with a higher average score.


**FCS survey results by financial mindset category** :


- **Prefer AI:** 76.4
- **Hybrid:** 71.9
- **Prefer a real human:** 70.3


### **What This Suggests About AI and Decision-Making**


A few features of AI financial tools may help explain the pattern. They’re generally always accessible and respond right away to inquiries, whether it’s midnight on a weekend or midweek during business hours. The responses also tend to be confident and detailed, and users can often ask as many follow-up questions as they want.


That kind of access could plausibly deepen a person’s understanding of their finances and reinforce the habit of making independent decisions.


## **Why is AI-Driven Financial Confidence Risky?**


While AI can be ever-present and confidence-instilling, there’s a major drawback: It presents answers with confidence, whether those answers are accurate or not.


### **Acting on AI Advice Without Verification**


The burden of verification typically falls on AI tool users, but they don’t always perform their due diligence. Of the 14% who prefer financial advice from AI, about 71% report they’ve followed AI advice without verifying it. That drops sharply to 44% for hybrid users and 33% for those who prefer a real human advisor.


This suggests that most of those who prefer AI advice tend to act on it without verification at some point.


### **When Confidence Reduces Caution**


All 3 financial mindset groups were relatively confident, scoring over 70 on the FCS scale, and 64% said they typically verify financial advice using other sources before acting.


However, the group that prefers AI advice was slightly more confident but also much less likely to validate AI financial guidance. As a result, they’re more likely to act on unverified advice.


## **When Do People Trust Human Advisors Over AI?**


The data shows that preferences for AI vs. human intelligence for financial guidance preferences shift depending on what’s at stake. But even when people lean human, AI often still has a role to play behind the scenes.


### **Trust Shifts Under Pressure**


Across scenarios in the survey, respondents leaned more heavily on human advisors as the financial stakes and emotional weight climbed. Here are a few examples.


#### **Market Downturn (high-stakes, emotional):**


When asked who they would consult first if their retirement account dropped 20%, 52% of respondents said a human financial professional. Of the remaining respondents, 29% said they’d prefer to consult both an AI-powered financial tool and a financial professional, 10% would decide independently, and 9% would turn to an AI-powered tool alone.


#### **Windfall Scenario (important but less stressful):**


When asked who they’d consult first after unexpectedly receiving a $250,000 windfall, the largest share of respondents (37%) again chose a human financial professional. Beyond that, 28% said they would decide independently, 26% would consult both an AI tool and a financial professional, and 10% would rely on AI alone.


The biggest shift here is that 15% fewer respondents would turn to a human advisor after a windfall compared to a market downturn, while 18% more would decide independently.


#### **General Preferences**


When asked which financial topics they feel most comfortable relying on primarily for AI guidance, respondents said budgeting, spending, travel, and vacation planning. Confidence in AI declined for more complex or emotional decisions, such as retirement planning, homebuying, and family planning.


Overall, users tend to rely on human advisors as the stakes increase, especially in the case of a sudden monetary loss. Conversely, they’re more likely to rely on themselves or AI for lower-risk situations.


### **Where AI Still Adds Value in High-Stakes Decisions**


A preference for human guidance doesn’t mean AI sits on the sidelines. Even in the market downturn scenario, where respondents leaned most heavily toward human advisors, 38% still wanted AI involved in some capacity (29% alongside a human professional, 9% on its own). That’s a meaningful share of people who see AI as part of the answer, even when the stakes are at their highest.


Inside that hybrid space, AI tools can support human advisors in several ways:


- Double-checking the math behind a recommendation, from retirement projections to tax scenarios
- Surfacing patterns in a person’s financial history that might otherwise take hours to find
- Stress-testing decisions against different market conditions or assumptions
- Pulling together the background data an advisor needs before a conversation, so the human time is spent on judgment rather than legwork


In other words, the preference for human advisors in emotional or complex moments doesn’t replace AI — it changes AI’s role from decision-maker to decision-support. That’s consistent with the broader hybrid pattern this study surfaces: AI handles speed and scale, humans handle context and judgment, and the combination tends to outperform either one alone.


### **Many AI Users Are Validating Information**


Many of those who prefer using AI in some capacity aren’t using it in isolation. When asked what they would do if AI suggested a tax strategy their financial advisor hadn’t mentioned, 60% of respondents would research it first. Further, 64% said they usually review or validate financial advice they receive from any source with other sources.


While hybrid users don’t have an average FCS as high as that of those who prefer AI, they’re much more likely to validate financial advice from AI, suggesting their confidence may be more justified.


## **Why Do People Ask AI Financial Questions They Won’t Ask Humans?**


Another notable benefit of AI financial tools is that they don’t require users to confess their financial circumstances to another person.


### **AI as a Judgment-Free Financial Tool**


The absence of a human on the other end of the conversation appears to lower the bar for asking sensitive questions. Without the social pressure that comes with sitting across from an advisor, people can raise topics they might otherwise avoid. In fact, 29% of respondents said they’ve asked AI a financial question they felt uncomfortable asking a person.


### **People Still Feel More Comfortable Asking a Human**


Although almost a third of respondents have asked AI something they didn’t want to ask a person, AI isn’t generally the preferred resource for financial questions. Our study showed that 47% of people generally prefer asking another person financial questions, compared to 21% who prefer asking AI, and 32% who feel equally comfortable asking either. However, this shows that AI can come in handy for those one-off questions people would rather not ask their advisors.


## **What Builds Trust in AI Financial Tools?**


AI financial tools are powerful, but their shortcomings still leave many users understandably skeptical. Here’s what users say could help build confidence in using them.


### **Top Factors Driving Trust**


When asked what would increase their trust in AI-powered financial tools, respondents pointed first to proven accuracy, signaling concerns about whether AI can consistently deliver reliable guidance. Access to a human expert ranked second, reinforcing the appeal of hybrid support. Then came strong data privacy protections, highlighting concerns about sharing sensitive financial information with AI.


### **Trust Is Conditional**


Users want guardrails in place to help ensure the information from AI tools is accurate and beneficial for their situation. For example, these could include security protocols, oversight from human professionals, and endorsements from trusted brands.


## **The Future of Financial Decision-Making Is Hybrid**


With AI changing the way people make financial decisions, what will the future hold?


### **AI and Human Expertise Will Work Together**


AI is generally being integrated into financial decision-making, but isn’t replacing human guidance.


Nearly half of respondents (45%) predict AI will be used alongside financial professionals in the future. In comparison, just 23% think human professionals will remain the primary source of guidance, and 17% think AI will replace professionals.


Reliance on human advisors is also expected to remain heavier in high-stakes scenarios, such as retirement planning and market downturns.


### **The Rise of Augmented Decision-Making**


Based on Intuit’s 2026 research, hybrid AI and HI financial guidance is on track to become the dominant model for American households by 2030, with 45% of US adults already expecting this shift.


AI brings speed, scale, and accessibility, while human advisors contribute experience, context, and the ability to make nuanced judgment calls.


That combination is what builds genuine[financial intelligence](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/financial-intelligence/) . And it’s the future the largest share of respondents anticipate.


## **Putting Hybrid Financial Decision-Making into Practice with Intuit Intelligence**


The findings point toward a clear pattern: Americans expect AI capabilities and human expertise in their financial decisions.


[Intuit Intelligence](https://investors.intuit.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/1277/intuit-unveils-revolutionary-system-of-intelligence-to-help-businesses-grow-in-the-ai-era) reflects that same principle in how it works for business owners, drawing on the broader patterns of[AI in fintech](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/tech-innovation/fintech-artificial-intelligence/) . Unlike a general-purpose AI trained on the open internet, Intuit Intelligence is built on real financial and business data: Tens of millions of customers and 625,000 data attributes per business, as well as[70,000](https://investors.intuit.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/1272/intuit-rapidly-advances-genos-to-accelerate-development-of-agentic-ai-experiences-at-scale) tax and financial attributes per consumer, refined over 40 years of tax and accounting work. That grounding is paired with a network of over 13,000 trusted financial experts, plus a network over 650K accountant customers, including accounting firms and accountants, so the platform’s answers come from someone who can stand behind them. You can use conversational AI to access workflows for accounting, payments, bill pay, payroll, and more.


## **Methodology**


This study is based on a survey of 1,000 US adults aged 18 and older. Results are weighted to reflect the US population.


Respondents were segmented into 3 groups based on how they approach financial decision-making: those who prefer a real human, those who prefer AI, and those who use a combination of both (Hybrid). These segments were determined using a composite scoring model built from multiple scenario-based and behavioral questions, rather than a single self-reported preference.


The study also introduces a Financial Confidence Score, a composite index that measures how confident individuals feel about their financial decision-making. The score is based on responses to statements related to confidence, control, preparedness, and financial regret.


This approach allows for comparison between decision-making styles and how they relate to confidence and behavior.


---


*¹Intuit surveyed 1,000 US adults, who were not paid for their response, March 2026.*
